 Hundreds of flights cancelled across East Asia as Typhoon Champi roars toward Taiwan
 23 October 2026 Summary
 Taiwan is bracing for powerful Typhoon Champi, which is passing close to the island's east coast with torrential rains and gusts of up to 191 kph (119mph)
 Taiwanese authorities have urged people to stay away from coasts and mountains, and are evacuating residents on the north-east coast living near a landslide dam at risk of breaching in the storm
 Hundreds of flights in Taiwan and neighbouring Japan have been cancelled , affecting thousands of passengers
 At least one person has died in Taiwan after being swept away by waves, according to authorities
 Champi is the latest in a string of intense typhoons as a Super El Niño heats up the Pacific Ocean and fuels storms
 Media caption, Watch: Japan hit by heavy rain and powerful winds Live Reporting
 Edited by Joel Guinto, with reporting from Joyce Lee in Taipei, Benny Lu in Hong Kong, Kurumi Mori in Tokyo and Koh Ewe in Singapore
 Taiwan braces for worst of Champi on Saturday published at 09:47 BST 23 October 09:47 BST 23 October 
 Typhoon Champi has shut Taiwan and forced the cancellation of hundreds of flights as it churned closer to the island's north-east coast today.
 One person died and 171 others were injured , while thousands of households in Japan's Okinawa islands, just north of Taiwan, suffered power outages. 
 But the worst of the typhoon is yet to come as it's forecast to bring up to 90cm (35in) of rain until Saturday. 
 After passing over north-east Taiwan, Champi is forecast to hover close to Okinawa , then China's eastern coast, before manoeuvering north-east towards mainland Japan.
 We'll be ending our live coverage shortly but you can read more on this story here . 
 Image source, CIRA and JMA/JAXA/Reuters

 'We're worried that our home will be flooded' published at 09:33 BST 23 October 09:33 BST 23 October 
 Residents of the coastal city Keelung in north-east Taiwan say they're worried the typhoon will flood their homes and businesses. 
 "Keelung has seen a lot of flooding this year. So we're worried that our home
will be flooded, that would be a hassle," says Liu Yu-En, an 18-year-old construction worker.
 Business owner Chang Ju-Pin, 55, is also concerned about the impact of the typhoon. 
 "Here in Keelung it seems that typhoons don't tend to be that big, but the flooding can be more severe," he tells Reuters. 
 Image source, Reuters Image caption, Chang Ju-Pin says typhoons aren't usually that big in Keelung

 Power outages affect 8,400 households in Okinawa published at 09:25 BST 23 October 09:25 BST 23 October 
 Approximately 8,400 households in Japan's southernmost Okinawa islands are experiencing power outages as of 14:00 local time (06:00 BST), according to a local energy provider. , external 
 Champi is forecast to pass close to Okinawa after grazing Taiwan's north-eastern coast.
 Okinawa Electric Power Company says strong winds and rain have made resoration work dangerous.
 Earlier today, the company said that 3,630 households were experiencing power outages because of the typhoon.

 One dead, 171 injured in Taiwan - authorities published at 09:09 BST 23 October 09:09 BST 23 October 
 I-ting Chiang 
BBC Chinese 
 Taiwan's Fire Department said that as of 15:00 local time, Typhoon Champi has caused one death and 171 injuries so far, a jump from the 94 injured reported earlier.
 Authorities said many of the injuries were traffic-related, including falling from motorcycles, followed by falls, and being hit by falling or tilted objects such as billboards or trees.
 Nine of the injured are foreign nationals: five Vietnamese, two Indonesians, and two Malaysians.

 Typhoon Champi swirls closer to north-east Taiwan - what's the latest? published at 08:49 BST 23 October 08:49 BST 23 October 
 Image source, Reuters It's mid-afternoon in Taiwan, where torrential rains and fierce wind gusts are predicted to hit the island's north-east as Typhoon Champi moves closer - here's the latest:
 It is unclear if the eye or centre of Champi will hit land, but it is forecast to bring up to 90cm (35in) of rain until Saturday, when its worst effects are expected.
 After grazing Taiwan's north-east coast, Champi is forecast to pass close to Japan's southern Okinawa islands, then China eastern coast, before turning north-east to the direction of mainland Japan
 Authorities have issued urgent safety warnings, advising the public to avoid high-risk zones, such as coasts and mountains 
 Disaster officials say one person died on Thursday after being swept away by waves in Liuqiu, a small island south-west of Taiwan's main island
 The storm has also injured 94 people , according to the fire department, with many of those injuries from traffic accidents and falls 
 Hundreds of flights have been cancelled across East Asia, affecting thousands of passengers 
 China's meteorological authority has issued a "blue" alert for Typhoon Champi - the lowest level in its four-tier warning system
 In Japan, 8,400 people are experiencing power outages due to the impact of the typhoon, according to Okinawa Electric Power

 Heaviest rainfall expected tomorrow morning published at 08:15 BST 23 October 08:15 BST 23 October 
 Benny Lu 
BBC Chinese, reporting from Hong Kong 
 Image source, Getty Images Taiwan's Central Weather Administration continues to issue warnings for both sea and land as Typhoon Champi approaches.
 Champi is currently located southeast of Yilan, moving northwest and then northeast. Its storm circle is gradually enveloping Taiwan, posing a threat to the country and outlying islands such as Penghu.
 The Central Weather Bureau says Champi is expected to slow down as it moves towards the north-east coast from this afternoon to evening, and may even exhibit irregular movements such as circling.
 Therefore, the current assessment is that the chance of it making landfall is not high.
 Rainfall is expected to be most significant tomorrow morning, and the storm will move away from the island by tomorrow night.

 What's in a typhoon name? published at 07:45 BST 23 October 07:45 BST 23 October 
 Image source, EPA/Shutterstock Typhoons get their names from a list compiled by the World Meteorological Organization, an agency of the UN.
 The names are submitted by member countries.
 Some, like Dolphin, are in English. Some are in the local language, like Chan-hom (a Laotian tree), Peilou (a migratory bird in Macau) and Nangka (the Malay name for jackfruit).
 Countries like the Philippines give typhoons their own local names because of the sheer number of storms that affect the country every year.
 Filipino meteorologists are referring to Typhoon Champi as Rosal - the local name for the gardenia plant.
 Typhoon names can be recycled for different storms, but are usually retired after they cause serious destruction, like Typhoon Haiyan (or Yolanda in the Philippines), which killed more than 6,000 people in 2013; or Typhoon Fung-wong ( Uwan in the Philippines), which killed dozens when it struck the Philippines and Taiwan last November.

 Photos from Taiwan as region braces for Typhoon Champi published at 07:12 BST 23 October 07:12 BST 23 October 
 We can now bring you more pictures from Keelung, a major port city in north-eastern Taiwan. 
 Residents have been warned by Taiwan's Central Weather Bureau to expect "torrential or extremely torrential rain" in the city. 
 Image source, Reuters Image source, Getty Images Image source, Reuters

 What does El Niño have to do with these typhoons? published at 06:59 BST 23 October 06:59 BST 23 October 
 Earlier we reported that this has been an unusually hectic typhoon season for the region .
 But it's not just typhoons. Recent months have seen a range of extreme weather events around the world.
 The eastern Pacific is seeing above average hurricane activity
 Indonesia has been battling its worst wildfire season in more than a decade, as its forests become drier and hotter
 Reduced monsoon rainfall is threatening agriculture in India
 Much of this is because of an exceptionally strong El Niño - a naturally occurring event that happens once every few years and lasts for around a year.
 During this period, trade winds in the Pacific Ocean can weaken or reverse, allowing warm water to spread eastwards.
 The heat from the ocean lifts global temperatures and changes rainfall patterns.
 The UK Met Office said this is shaping up to be the "largest El Niño in living memory". This means 2027 is likely going to be the world's hottest year on record, the agency said.

 While landfall is unclear, hazards remain published at 06:41 BST 23 October 06:41 BST 23 October 
 Image source, Getty Images Weather forecasters may be unsure if Champi will make landfall in Taiwan, but the hazards from the storm, one of the strongest on the planet this year, remain.
 Taiwan's weather agency forecasts that up to 90cm (35in) will fall from Thursday to Saturday, with the north-east coast expected to be the hardest-hit. 
 "People should be aware that the strong winds and extremely heavy rain will continue into the first half of tomorrow (Saturday)," Central Weather Administration administrator Lu Kuo-chen says.
 A typhoon has technically made landfall when its centre or eye moves from the sea onto land, according to Taiwan's weather agency.
 Across the Asia region, however, many typhoons have caused widespread damage even when the eye has not made landfall.
 Storms that skirt coastlines are capable of stirring torrential rains and strong winds that cause floods and landslides.

 Will Typhoon Champi make landfall in Taiwan? published at 06:24 BST 23 October 06:24 BST 23 October 
 We reported earlier that Taiwanese authorities were warning people to stay alert as the island braced for Typhoon Champi to make landfall.
 But for now, it remains unclear if the storm will make landfall in Taiwan or just brush past the island's coast as it heads northwards to Japan.
 Forecasts by the meteorological agencies in Taiwan and Japan show that the eye of the storm is expected to skirt past Taiwan's northeastern tip without making landfall.
 But a forecaster from Taiwan's Central Weather Administration also told Reuters that they could not rule out landfall, if the storm "stalls, loops, or wobbles from side to side" as it approaches Taiwan.

 Champi batters the Philippines' northern islands published at 06:10 BST 23 October 06:10 BST 23 October 
 As Champi moves closer to Taiwan, it is also stirring heavy rains and strong winds in Batanes, a Philippine island chain located between southern Taiwan and Luzon, the Philippines' main northern island.
 The second-highest in a five-step wind warning system has been raised in the Batanes islands. This means 150km/h winds are expected.
 Photos posted on the local government's Facebook page showed waves crashing into seaside villages and roads closed to traffic. There were no immediate reports of casualties.
 While it is affected by many of the 20 or so tropical storms in the Philippines every year, communities in Batanes are reputed to be more resilient against inclement weather. Many homes are made of thick limestone, engineered to withstand typhoon winds.
 Champi has hovered in waters north-east of the Philippines for days. It is known locally as Typhoon Rosal.
 Image source, DPWH-BDEO Philippines/Facebook

 Champi was this year's strongest storm published at 05:41 BST 23 October 05:41 BST 23 October 
 A few days ago, Typhoon Champi officially became the strongest storm of the year. 
 On Tuesday afternoon, it attained a maximum sustained wind speed of 185mph (298km/h) as it moved over the Philippine sea - the equivalent of a Category 5 hurricane.
 Typhoon Champi was initially categorised as a "super typhoon", which is when a cyclone's sustained wind speed reaches 240 km/h(150 mph).
 The typhoon appeared to weaken on Wednesday as it continued travelling through the sea.
 But it remains powerful, carrying sustained winds of 155km/h (96mph) near its centre around noon on Friday, according to Taiwan's weather authorities.

 Japan cancels more than 160 flights published at 05:20 BST 23 October 05:20 BST 23 October 
 Kurumi Mori 
Tokyo correspondent 
 More than 160 flights have been cancelled across four Japanese airlines. 
 Japanese airline All Nippon Airways (ANA) just said all flights departing from and arriving at Miyako Airport and Ishigaki Airport, in the southern Okinawa prefecture, are canceled for the entire day.
 It also says operations being impacted at Okhotsk Monbetsu, Okinawa Naha Airport, Tsushima, Miyazaki, and Kagoshima Airports.
 In an update moments ago, Japan Airlines said it had cancelled flights to Taipei Songshan Airport and Taiwan Taoyuan International Airport.

 Power outages in more than 3,600 household in Okinawa published at 04:57 BST 23 October 04:57 BST 23 October 
 Kurumi Mori 
Tokyo correspondent 
 Here in Japan, 3,630 households are experiencing power outages due to the impact of the typhoon, according to Okinawa Electric Power.
 The company says the strong rain and wind are creating dangerous conditions for outdoor work, so they’re conducting restoration work via remote operation.
 I’m in Tokyo, where it’s just cloudy, but forecasts call for four straight rainy days starting tomorrow.
 Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has warned people to remain alert to the typhoon, telling them to "exercise extreme caution against storm-force winds, high waves, sediment disasters and storm surges through tomorrow". 
 "Vigilance is also needed against flooding in low-lying areas, as well as rising and overflowing rivers" in the Okinawa and Amami regions, she wrote in a post on X.
 Many have replied to Takaichi's post, thanking her for keeping them updated on social media as fewer people are watching TV or reading newspapers.

 China issues low-level alert for Typhoon Champi published at 04:39 BST 23 October 04:39 BST 23 October 
 China's meteorological authority has issued a "blue" alert for Typhoon Champi - the lowest level in its four-tier warning system.
 The storm is expected to skirt past the country's eastern coast over the coming weekend.
 The agency is warning of strong winds and rainfall of 50-80mm along its eastern coast, including Shanghai.
 Zhejiang Province, which is set to be the country's worst-hit by the storm, has issued an "orange" alert - the second-highest level - warning of huge waves along its coast.

 Taiwan shuts schools and offices across island published at 04:14 BST 23 October 04:14 BST 23 October 
 I-ting Chiang 
BBC Chinese 
 Image source, AFP via Getty Images Work and classes have been suspended in nearly all of Taiwan's 22 counties and cities on Friday as Typhoon Champi approaches the island.
 Only Kinmen County, an archipelago located to the west of Taiwan's mainland, will continue work and classes as usual.
 Taiwan's stock exchange - one of the largest in the world - is also closed today.
 The island is starting to experience heavy rainfall, with some areas in Taipei City already accumulating more than 200mm of rainfall within 24 hours.
 The Central Weather Administration predicts that Typhoon Champi's storm circle will continue battering Taiwan until Saturday evening.
 Strong winds are expected in the island's northern region, with wind gusts reaching up to level 12, the highest on the Beaufort scale. Authorities are warning people to stay away from beaches and mountains.
 Share close panel Share page Copy link About sharing 
 Typhoon Champi forecast to sweep northwards published at 03:57 BST 23 October 03:57 BST 23 October 
 Typhoon Champi is currently moving in a northwesterly direction towards Taiwan, where residents are bracing for powerful winds and rain forecast throughout Friday and Saturday.
 By Saturday afternoon, the typhoon is expected to swerve away from China's eastern coast and head for Japan.
 Share close panel Share page Copy link About sharing 
 Taiwan cancels nearly 1,000 flights published at 03:44 BST 23 October 03:44 BST 23 October 
 Authorities in Taiwan have cancelled all 262 domestic flights and more than 660 international ones scheduled for Friday, local media report.
 Railway and ferry services have also been suspended, while some highways have been closed ahead of the powerful storm.
 Share close panel Share page Copy link About sharing 
 Person died after being swept away by waves - Taiwan authorities published at 03:28 BST 23 October 03:28 BST 23 October 
 Now bringing you more details on the typhoon casualties reported in Taiwan.
 According to a press briefing Taiwan's disaster authorities, one person died yesterday after being swept away by waves in Liuqiu, a small coral island southwest of Taiwan's main island.
 The storm has also injured 94 people, according to the fire department. Many of those injuries were from traffic accidents and falls, authorities say.
